claims.text: Low hardness and strength in the as-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi solid solution are governed jointly by facile homogeneous dislocation glide and dynamic recovery.
The matrix is sparse in obstacles and effectively free of precipitate or secondary-phase barriers to dislocation motion.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the proposed state has high stacking-fault energy.
High stacking-fault energy enables facile dislocation glide and discourages dislocation locking and deformation twinning.
Dynamic recovery continually rearranges or annihilates dislocations during loading.
Dynamic recovery limits dislocation accumulation and pile-ups, thereby limiting strain hardening, hardness, and strength.
The starting material is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state with controlled, uniform grain size.
Dislocation activity occurs along multiple {110} slip planes.
Room-temperature testing over strain rates of approximately 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1 and strains up to 5–10% can probe the proposed mechanism.
In situ TEM, synchrotron X-ray diffraction, EBSD, and X-ray line-profile analysis can be combined to measure dislocation motion, density, arrangement, and recovery.
In situ TEM will show uniform dislocation motion with little dislocation tangling.
Deformation will produce minimal evidence of twin formation.
Diffraction and post-deformation measurements will show relatively low dislocation densities and prominent signatures of dynamic recovery.
Dynamic-recovery signatures will be more prominent at lower strain rates.
Higher strain rates may produce a modest increase in strain hardening.
The unmodified alloy will retain lower hardness and yield strength than variants containing nanoscale precipitate obstacles.
The proposed mechanism is limited to defect-sparse, single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested at room temperature, at strains up to about 10%, and at strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1.
Introducing controlled nanoscale precipitates should increase dislocation pinning, strain hardening, hardness, and strength relative to the unmodified state.

contradictions.description: The material is repeatedly described as as-cast, but the initial-state field says that it is produced through casting and thermo-mechanical processing. A thermo-mechanically processed specimen is not strictly an as-cast specimen.

The specified {110} slip planes conventionally suggest a BCC slip description, whereas the high-stacking-fault-energy argument about suppressing twinning is normally framed for FCC slip on {111} planes. No crystal structure is stated to reconcile these descriptions.
